name: Eagle Beach
label: Eagle Beach
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Eagle Beach' (4 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-17: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Wide white sand beach with the iconic fofoti trees.

text.description:
Eagle Beach, also known as Arend Beach, is a beach and neighbourhood of Oranjestad, and it is the widest beach in Aruba. The sand is soft and white, and the resorts behind it are low-rise, so the sky and the horizon stay open. It has been rated one of the best beaches in the world. The beach is public, so you can walk along it freely.

The picture most visitors come for is the wind-bent fofoti trees leaning over the white sand, with the turquoise sea behind them. Guides often call the trees the most photographed subject on the island. They make a strong dark shape against a bright sky, which is why the view works so well at sunset.

Walk along the sand until the trees sit clearly against the sea, and keep a little distance so the whole curve of each tree fits in the frame. Include some empty sand in the foreground to give the picture depth. The fofoti trees are protected, so please don't hang anything on them and stay off their roots. Sea turtles nest on this beach from April to October, so don't use any lights near the nests at night. A short walk along the beach will give you plenty of different angles.
text.geographic_location: Eagle Beach is a beach and neighbourhood of Oranjestad, Aruba, lined with low-rise resorts.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or railway stops are nearby. The subject point lies about 360 m to the north-east, a short walk along the beach. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the classic view of the trees, sand and sea. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want to take in a whole tree and a big sky from close up. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a single tree against the sunset.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. As you line up the shot, the turquoise sea and the sunset sky come into the frame around the trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon on the top or bottom line, so the trees and sky have room. Keep a strip of empty sand in the foreground. For a silhouette, frame the tree against the brightest part of the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bright sky to focus and lower the exposure slider a little, so the trees go dark and the sky colour stays rich. Try a Live Photo too, as the leaves and waves move. Keep your phone away from the sea spray and wipe the lens before shooting.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: About 30 minutes before sunset, when the trees stand out against the orange sky. Sunrise also works well, with side light on the sand.

text.access_note: Eagle Beach is an open public beach, and turtle-nesting precautions apply from April to October.
claims_not_in_sources: Tapping on the sky and lowering the exposure slider will darken the trees into silhouettes on most phones.
Sea spray can get on a phone lens, so wipe it before shooting.

name: Palm Beach, Aruba
label: Palm Beach
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'De Palm Pier' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'De Palm Pier' (way/335257951): middle (48 m across); moved 20 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/378040153: large area 'Palm Beach' (1506 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.

text.description: Palm Beach is a tourism district in Aruba, lined with high-rise hotels around a long, pale beach with clear shallow water. It photographs well because of the colour. Turquoise water runs out to the horizon, and sailboats and seabirds often add a focal point. The best phone view is from De Palm Pier, the easy, quieter alternative to the busy hotel frontage. If you are at the pier, walk to the far end and face the sea. The water fills most of the frame and the pier's lines lead your eye towards the sunset, with the Palm Beach skyline along the shoreline. The name comes from a coconut plantation owned by Captain R.J. Beaujon, who named it after Palm Beach in Florida, and the beach was officially registered under that name in 1960. The first hotel here, opened in the 1950s, was a set of bungalows on bare sand, which is a long way from today's towers. If you want people in the shot, the Palm Beach Boardwalk is good for candid pictures of walkers among palm trees. Eduardo's Beach Shack has swings among palms with the sea behind, which suits a relaxed portrait. Eduardo's is on private business property, so you may only see it during opening hours. Go at sunrise or sunset for softer light and fewer people.
text.geographic_location: Palm Beach is a tourist district in Noord, about 6 km northwest of Oranjestad. It is a strip of beach and high-rise hotels on Aruba's coast, with a shopping district adjacent to the hotels.
text.directions_text: From Oranjestad, head northwest to the Palm Beach area, about 6 km away. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the pier, the water and the sky together. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, more natural view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a sailboat or seabirds on the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on De Palm Pier (walk to the far end of the pier, facing the sea). Turquoise water running to the horizon, with sailboats and seabirds framing the Palm Beach skyline behind the shoreline.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower third line. Let the pier's edge or railing lead the eye towards the sunset or the open water. Wait for a sailboat or a bird to enter the frame, rather than shooting an empty sea. For a different view, try the Palm Beach Boardwalk for people walking among palms.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the sea or sky to focus. Then drag the exposure slider down a little so the bright sky keeps its colour and the water stays rich. Keep the horizon level using the gridlines. Wipe the lens first, as sea spray and sunscreen smear it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise and sunset, when the light is softer and the crowds are thinner.

text.access_note: Access can change, so check locally before you go.

name: Druif Beach
label: Druif Beach
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q5309004: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Quiet beach on the west coast just north of the town.

text.description:
Druif Beach is a stretch of shoreline in Oranjestad, Aruba, about 300 metres long. That is long enough to give you a good sweep of coast, but short enough to walk end to end in a few minutes. It works well for phone photos because a beach gives you simple, clear layers: sand in the foreground, water in the middle and sky above. Those layers make an easy, uncluttered picture.

The phone icon on the map is about 450 m west of the subject. From there you can take a wider shot of the coast and the beach in its setting. Then walk along to the beach itself for closer pictures, such as a shot along the length of the sand or a low shot with the water's edge leading into the frame.

Whichever you choose, keep the horizon level, because on a long, flat view a tilted horizon is the first thing the eye notices. Turn on gridlines to help. If people are on the beach, wait a moment for a gap, or include them on purpose to show the scale. Conditions change from day to day, so take a few frames from different spots rather than relying on one.
text.geographic_location: Druif Beach is on the coast of Oranjestad, the capital of Aruba.
text.directions_text: From there, the beach is a short walk of roughly 450 metres to the east. Head east along the shore side and use the map to keep your bearings. The phone icon on the map is about 450 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the overall scene. Use the telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) from where you stand to bring the distant beach closer. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) once you are on the sand to fit in the full sweep of the shore.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 450 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. From here the beach is a distant feature, so treat this as a scene-setting view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: From where you stand, use gridlines and place the shoreline on the lower third, with plenty of sky above. Zoom to 2x or 3x if the beach looks too small. On the beach, stand near one end and shoot along the 300 m length so the line of the shore leads the eye through the frame. Keep the horizon level.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the sand or the sea to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the colours stay rich and the highlights are not washed out. If there is any movement in the water, try a Live Photo.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light than midday. Late in the afternoon the sun is behind you when looking east from where you stand, which helps light the scene evenly.

text.access_note: Check the official site or local signs before you go in case any access rules apply to the beach.

name: Royal Aruba Aloe
label: Aruba Aloe
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Pitastraat' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Pitastraat nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/96336745: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Aruba Aloe Museum and Factory' (65 m across).
notes: Aloe factory and museum on the road to the hotel area.

text.description:
Royal Aruba Aloe is a working aloe company with a small museum and store in Hato, Oranjestad. It is not a monument, so the pictures here are about the plants and the setting. The most rewarding frame is the aloe growing in the field beside the store, with the factory buildings behind if the view lines up on the ground. That would tell the story of the place in one shot: the crop, then the factory that processes it.

The company was founded in 1890 by Cornelis Eman and is still owned by the Eman family. The store beside the field opened in 2000, next to Eman's original aloe field. In 2021 the company received a Royal Predicate in recognition of its long history. The museum offers tours in English, Dutch, Spanish and Papiamento, and visitors can see parts of the production process. That makes the building frontage worth a second picture, with its aloe sign in view.

Start outside on Pitastraat as a quieter open-air alternative to the shop entrance. Confirm the view on the ground. If the field and buildings read together, take a wide shot of the field with the buildings behind, then move in on a single plant for a close-up. Keep the sign or the factory roofline in the background so the picture says where you are. Then, if you go in, photograph the frontage at the entrance as a second image. Check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements.
text.geographic_location: In Hato, Oranjestad, at Pitastraat 115. The photo stretch is next to the company's store and the original aloe field. Confirm the exact position on Pitastraat on site.
text.directions_text: No public transport is listed for this spot. The address is Pitastraat 115, Hato, Oranjestad. Once there, look for the store and the aloe field beside it. Confirm the view on the ground. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the field with the factory behind it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for the building frontage and sign if you are close. Use 2x or 3x if your phone has it for a tight shot of the plants with the buildings softly behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Pitastraat (stretch beside the store, next to Cornelis Eman's original aloe field). Aloe plants growing in the field beside the store, with the factory buildings in the background. Check on the ground whether the aloe plants and the factory buildings are visible together from here.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines. If the factory buildings are visible, put the aloe plants in the lower third and the buildings along the upper line so both read clearly. Crouch a little so the plants look larger against the buildings. For a variation, step closer to one plant and let the background blur behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the aloe leaves to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is washing out. For the close-up, try portrait mode so the buildings go soft.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before the heat, is the general advice from one guide for visiting fields. It is not a rule for this spot.

text.access_note: The field is next to the store, but the museum and store are a business, so check the official site before you go for visiting and tour arrangements. Confirm the Pitastraat view on site.

name: Bubali Bird Sanctuary
label: Bubali Bird Sanctuary
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Bubali Bird Sanctuary' (5 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q19275950: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Wetland reserve with an observation tower.

text.description:
Bubali Bird Sanctuary is a 20-hectare wetland at the north-western end of Aruba. It began life as a wastewater treatment facility and has since become an Important Bird Area, recognised by BirdLife International. Two connected ponds sit among reeds and desert scrub, and they attract coots, moorhens, white-cheeked pintails, green herons and a large roost of neotropic cormorants. It is an unusual place to photograph so close to the hotel strip: flat water, green reeds and birds, with the Old Dutch Windmill nearby.

The best photo vantage point is the wooden observation tower on the north side. It lifts you above the reeds, so you can take in both ponds and the birds on and above the water, including herons, egrets, coots and ducks. The wetland is quite open, so the birds are often small in the frame. Take a wide shot of the whole scene first, then zoom in on one bird or group rather than trying to capture everything at once.

About 24% of the area burned in September 2018. Some visitors say the tower is worn and that hornets can nest around the stairs, so use your judgement on the climb and keep a little distance from any nests. Keep your phone's flash off so you don't disturb the birds.
text.geographic_location: The sanctuary is in Noord, in the north-west of Aruba, a short distance north of central Oranjestad rather than inside it. The observation tower is on its north side, opposite the Old Dutch Windmill and close to the high-rise hotels.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stops serve this spot. From central Oranjestad, head north towards the hotel area in Noord; it is a short drive. Look for the Bubali Bird Sanctuary or the Old Dutch Windmill, which stands opposite the tower. Once there, the observation tower is on the north side of the wetland. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the wide view of both ponds from the tower. Switch to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out herons, egrets or coots. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want the tower rail or the sky to take up more of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. The wooden observation tower on the north side, opposite the Old Dutch Windmill, is the recommended vantage point nearby. From the top you look out over the two connected wetland ponds, with herons, egrets, coots and ducks visible above the vegetation.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the waterline on the lower third, so the reeds and ponds fill the middle and the sky the top. Take one wide shot of the whole wetland, then zoom in on a single bird or small group. Keep the tower rail out of the frame by holding the phone just above it. Once you are on the tower, the viewpoint is not a place for portrait mode; it works better for wide scenes.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest bird or the water to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little if the sky washes out. Keep the flash off. For moving birds, hold the shutter button for a burst, or use Live Photos/motion and pick the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when guides say the birds are most active and the light is softer.

text.access_note: The tower is reported to be free to use and there are no known closures, but check the official site before you go, as visitors report the tower is in poor repair.
claims_not_in_sources: The sanctuary lies in Noord, a short drive north of central Oranjestad, not in Oranjestad itself.
The observation tower is on the north side, opposite the Old Dutch Windmill, and is free to use.
The tower is close to the high-rise hotels.
Some visitors report the tower is in poor repair, and hornets may nest around the stairs.
Flash photography may disturb the birds and is best avoided.
Birds are most active, and the light softer, early in the morning and late in the afternoon.
Birds appear small in the frame from the tower, so zooming helps.

name: National Archaeological Museum Aruba
label: Archaeological Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/368232024: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'National Archeological Museum Aruba' (89 m across).

text.description: The National Archaeological Museum Aruba is an archaeological museum in the city of Oranjestad, and it makes an easy stop if you are walking around town with your phone. It is dedicated to the island's early history, and its collections stretch from about 2500 BCE to the 19th century. The museum first opened in 1981 as the Archaeological Museum of Aruba. In 2009 it moved to a new location and reopened under its present name, the National Archaeological Museum Aruba. The Papiamento name, Museo Arqueologico Nacional Aruba, is worth knowing because you may see it on signs. For photographs, the appeal is the building and its setting rather than any one dramatic view. A plain frontage with the name on it gives you a tidy record of your visit, and the surrounding streets add a bit of Oranjestad atmosphere. The phone icon on the map is right at the museum, so you can shoot from the spot itself. The building is fairly wide, so you may need to step back to fit it in. Keep your phone level so the walls do not lean, and wait a moment for people to move out of the frame. Photography inside a museum is often limited, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In the city of Oranjestad, Aruba, on the site of the museum building itself.
text.directions_text: No public transport stops are listed for this spot. Navigate to the National Archaeological Museum (Museo Arqueologico Nacional Aruba) in Oranjestad. Once you are at the museum, the phone icon on the map is at the museum itself. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the building as you see it. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you cannot step back far enough to fit the whole frontage in.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Move back as far as is practical to fit the whole building in.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line them up with the edges of the building so the verticals stay straight. Include the museum's name or sign if you can, as it makes the photo easy to identify later. Use 2x if you want a closer shot of a doorway, sign or detail without walking into the road.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to set focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is bright, so the walls do not wash out. Hold the phone steady with both hands.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows than midday. Weekdays may be quieter, but check the museum's own times first.

text.access_note: This is a museum, so entry may be ticketed or restricted; check the official site before you go.

name: Fort Zoutman
label: Fort Zoutman
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/1755806903: the OpenStreetMap point 'Historical Museum'.
notes: Oldest building in Aruba, with the Willem III Tower and the Historical Museum.

text.description:
Fort Zoutman is an old military fortification in Oranjestad, and it now houses the Historical Museum of Aruba. The fort dates from the 18th and 19th centuries, so you are photographing a building with real age, not a modern copy. Inside, the museum explains the history of the island and its people, in both rural and urban areas. It has been run by the Fundacion Museo Arubano (the Aruban Museum Foundation) since 1992.

It works well as a photo because it is a solid, simple structure with strong shapes. Walls, edges and any defensive details give you clean lines, and the plain surfaces make a good contrast with Aruba's bright sky. It is a good record shot to show where you were in town, and an easy one to take in passing.

Stand there, turn towards the north-east, and take the whole building in one frame first. Then move a few steps closer for details such as the entrance, the stonework or the way the walls meet. Keep your phone straight so the vertical lines do not lean.
text.geographic_location: Fort Zoutman is in the town of Oranjestad, Aruba. The Historical Museum of Aruba is housed inside the fort.
text.directions_text: Head for Oranjestad and look for Fort Zoutman (the Historical Museum). No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. The phone icon on the map is about 35 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole fort. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the building does not fit from where you are standing, or use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details in the walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 35 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. From here the fort should be in front of you as a whole building, so you can frame it without moving much.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the main walls with them to keep the vertical lines straight. Leave a little sky above the building so it does not look cramped. Take a second, closer photo of one detail, such as the entrance or the stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the fort to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the walls keep their colour and the sky does not wash out.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and gentler shadows on the walls. Midday sun can be harsh in Aruba, so use the exposure slider if you visit then.

text.access_note: The fort houses a museum, so entry to the inside may be ticketed or restricted; check the official site before you go.

notes: Colourful Dutch colonial parliament building in the town centre.

text.description:
The Parliament of Aruba is the building shown on this map spot, and it is in Oranjestad. It works well as a straightforward 'building in its setting' photo: you can see the whole front from a short distance, so there is no need to crop tightly or hunt for an odd angle.

The phone icon on the map is about 50 m south-east of the subject. That is close enough to fill the frame and far enough back to keep the whole building in view without tilting your phone upwards. Take one wide shot with the default lens (1x) to show the building and what surrounds it. Then take a second, closer one with the telephoto lens (2x or more) to pick out the entrance and the architectural details. If you stand a little to one side, the building looks more three-dimensional than it does straight on.

Turn on the gridlines and line up the roof and wall edges with them, so the verticals stay straight. Cars, passers-by and street furniture may drift into the frame, so take a few shots and keep the cleanest. Because this is a working government building, stay on public ground, be considerate of staff and visitors, and follow any signs.
text.geographic_location: In Oranjestad, 52 m south-east of the building at the stand-here point.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. The phone icon on the map is about 50 m south-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole building. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the entrance and details. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if passers-by or traffic force you to stand closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 50 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line up the building's vertical edges with them so the walls stay straight. Keep the phone level and held at chest height rather than tilted upwards. Take one wide frame with its surroundings and one tighter frame on the entrance.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the walls keep their colour and the sky does not wash out.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is usually kinder to a building front than harsh midday sun. Check which way the front faces, as the light will differ from one side to the other.

name: Paardenbaai
label: Paardenbaai Harbour
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q21972950: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Main harbour and cruise terminal with the waterfront promenade.

text.description:
Paardenbaai, which means Bay of Horses, is the main passenger seaport of Aruba and the working waterfront of Oranjestad. The name goes back to the days when horses were shipped from here to Jamaica and other places. Oranjestad itself grew up around this harbour, which has been in use since 1796, and the nearby Fort Zoutman dates from the same year. Today the port handles passengers only: cargo was moved to Barcadera (the move was completed in 2015 and Barcadera opened in 2016), and Paardenbaai has been passengers-only since 2016. That makes it a lively, tidy place to photograph, with ships alongside the quay and people coming and going.

For a phone photo, the appeal is the mix of water, ships and town in one frame. Use the whole scene rather than a single detail: a ship's hull against the sky, the line of the quay leading the eye along the water, and the colours of the waterfront behind. Stand back a little so you can include some foreground, such as the quayside or railings, to give the picture depth. Keep the horizon level using the gridlines. If a large ship fills the view, step back along the quay or switch to the ultra-wide lens so it fits. Be aware that this is a working port, so follow any signs and staff instructions about where you may walk and photograph.
text.geographic_location: Paardenbaai is the harbour area of Oranjestad, on the town's waterfront. Part of the port now lies in the Taratata area, on land reclaimed in the 1920s.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from the centre of Oranjestad and head to the harbour front. It is about 3 minutes on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 190 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full harbour scene and big ships, then use the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a single ship or detail across the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 190 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the horizon on a gridline and keep it level. Include a strip of quayside or railing in the foreground to lead the eye towards the ships, and leave some sky above. If the view is wide, a panorama can take in the whole waterfront; hold the phone steady and move slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the water to focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly if bright sky washes out the picture. Turn on gridlines to keep the horizon straight.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the water. Check which ships are in port, as the view changes from day to day.

text.access_note: The harbour is a working passenger port, open day and night, but some areas may be restricted, so check the official site before you go.

The number and size of ships in port changes from day to day.

name: Protestant Church (Aruba)
label: Protestant Church
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Wilhelminastraat' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Wilhelminastraat nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/6251083: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Old Protestant Church' (56 m across).
notes: Historic 19th-century church in the town centre.

text.description:
The Protestant Church in Oranjestad is really two buildings side by side, and the one name is often used for both. The larger church was inaugurated on 28 May 1950 and was designed by C.M. Bakker. Next to it stands the old church from 1846, the second oldest surviving building in Oranjestad after Fort Zoutman. A tower was added to the old church in 1867. The congregation still holds services in Papiamento.

It photographs well because the pale walls and the tower stand out against a clear sky, and the street gives you a straight, simple view. Visitors often shoot it from below, because the church is usually closed to the public. The old church was restored in 1988 and now serves as an exhibition and concert hall. It also houses the A. van den Doel Bible Museum.

It is on Wilhelminastraat, in front of number 1, with the church just to the north. Look up at the tower and facade, keep the lines straight with the gridlines, and leave some sky around the top. For a quieter second picture, move along to the older 1846 building. Its portico has the year 1846 worked into the ironwork, which makes a good close-up.
text.geographic_location: In Oranjestad, on Wilhelminastraat, where the 1950 church and the older 1846 church stand next to each other. It is reached from L.G. Smith Boulevard.
text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this spot. Head to Wilhelminastraat in Oranjestad, reached from L.G. Smith Boulevard, and walk from there. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x). If you are close and the tower will not fit, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x). Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details such as the portico and the 1846 ironwork on the older building.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Wilhelminastraat (in front of Wilhelminastraat 1, looking up at the church and its tower from the street). The church's tall tower and facade rising against the blue sky, framed from the pavement in front of the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the tower with a vertical line so the building does not look as if it leans. Tilting the phone upwards makes the sides lean inwards, so step back a little if you can, and keep a band of sky above the top. If you want a second picture, the older 1846 church beside it has a portico on the Wilhelminastraat side with the year 1846 in the ironwork. Check which building you are photographing, because the two stand side by side.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the blue sky stays deep and the white walls do not wash out. Take a few frames, as the tower's lean changes with every small tilt.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a clear day, when the sky behind the tower is blue. Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the walls.

text.access_note: The church is usually locked and is best photographed from the street, so check the official site before you go if you hope to see inside or visit the Bible Museum.

name: City Hall (Oranjestad)
label: City Hall
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Wilhelminastraat' (1 web pages); placed at the stretch of Wilhelminastraat nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/38755794: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'City Hall' (27 m across).
notes: Dutch colonial town hall next to Fort Zoutman.

text.description: City Hall, also known as the Eloy Arends House (Stadhuis in Dutch), is a colonial-style building in the middle of Oranjestad. It started life as a home. Doctor Jacobo Eloy Maria Arends had it built on a large plot in the centre of town for his bride, and the couple married in 1925. The architect was Chibi Wever, and the design drew on South American Neo-Baroque. Today the building handles civil registration, passports and weddings, and it is a popular place for couples to marry. It was restored in 1997, and another major restoration followed in 2014. That history helps explain the rich detail you can photograph: coral-stone walls, carved balconies, shutters and arched windows. This spot suits a quieter, more textured shot than the straight-on front view. Walk the block between Wilhelminastraat and Caya G.F. Betico Croes and shoot along the side wall and facade. In low morning light the stone, the balcony carvings and the tile-lined sidewalk all show up well. If you want the full lime-green front with its white balconies, the straight-on front view of the Stadhuis is the alternative. Because the building is used for weddings, be considerate with the entrance and anyone nearby. Photos of couples or the doorway may be restricted, so keep your pictures to the architecture.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Oranjestad, on the block between Wilhelminastraat and Caya G.F. Betico Croes. The building stands on a large plot in the middle of town.
text.directions_text: Head for the centre of Oranjestad and ask for the Stadhuis (City Hall), listed at Wilhelminastraat 8. Walk slowly along the block so you can look at the side wall and facade before you pick your spot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the facade and side wall together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the pavement is too narrow to fit the building in. Use 2x or more to pick out balcony carvings and details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Wilhelminastraat (the block between Wilhelminastraat and Caya G.F. Betico Croes, shooting along the building's side wall and facade). The building's facade and side in low morning light, with the coral-stone walls, balcony carvings and tile-lined sidewalk visible.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the side wall up with one of them so the street leads the eye towards the facade. Let the tiled sidewalk fill the foreground. Then step in for a tighter shot of the carved balconies. For the full lime-green front with its white balconies, shutters and arched windows, take the Stadhuis front view as a second shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the wall to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the light stone does not wash out. Keep the phone level so the vertical lines stay straight.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning, when low light picks out the texture of the walls and carvings.

text.access_note: The building is open to visitors only during working hours and is used for civil weddings, so photos of couples or the entrance may be restricted; check the official site before you go.

name: St. Francis of Assisi Church, Oranjestad
label: St. Francis Church
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q23662587: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.

text.description:
St. Francis of Assisi Church is a Catholic church in the city of Oranjestad, on the island of Aruba. It serves as the pro-cathedral, which means a temporary cathedral, and it belongs to the Diocese of Willemstad. It was built in 1829 and is counted among the most important churches on the island. Services are held in Papiamento and English, so it is a working place of worship as well as a landmark.

For a phone photographer, the appeal is a single, clear building that can be shown as a whole, with the sky behind it. The phone icon on the map is about 450 m north of the subject. That is a short walk, so you will be photographing it as part of a stroll through town rather than from one fixed spot. Move around a little: a straight-on shot gives a calm, symmetrical picture, while a slight angle shows more of the walls and the depth of the building.

Keep your distance where you can, so the church fits in the frame without the phone tilting upwards. If you must tilt, the buildings will lean inwards, so use the gridlines to keep the vertical edges straight. Because this is an active church, be considerate of anyone arriving for a service, and check locally before you go if you would like to see inside.
text.geographic_location: The church is in Oranjestad, on the Caribbean island of Aruba.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or railway stops are listed for this spot, so start from the phone icon on the map, or from the centre of Oranjestad, and head south. The church is about 446 m away in a straight line, a short walk. The phone icon on the map is about 450 m north of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole church. If you are close or the street is narrow, try the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit it in. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the facade or the top of the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 450 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south. Walk south towards the church and pick a place with a clear view of the front, ideally with some distance so you don't have to tilt the phone upwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the vertical edges of the church with them. Keep the building central for a calm, balanced shot, or step to one side for an angled view. Leave some sky above, and avoid cutting off the top.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the church to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the walls keep their detail. Avoid tilting the phone upwards, as it makes the building lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light than midday, and the sun is lower. Avoid taking photographs during a service.

text.access_note: This is a working place of worship, so dress modestly and respectfully if you go in, and check locally before you go for any visiting arrangements.

name: Trams in Oranjestad
label: Oranjestad Streetcar
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Caya Betico Croes' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'caya betico croes 210A' (node/11990614069): point; moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q1848105: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Heritage streetcar running along the harbour front.

text.description: Oranjestad's tram is a small, heritage-style streetcar that glides along the pedestrian-only main shopping street, and that is what makes it fun to photograph. The cars are painted in bold colours (green, orange, blue and red), so they stand out against the colonial-style buildings on both sides of the street. It is the first and so far the only passenger rail service on Aruba and in the Dutch Caribbean, and it was inaugurated on 22 December 2012, with regular service starting on 19 February 2013. The cars run on batteries and hydrogen fuel cells instead of overhead wires, so you get a clean line of sky above the tram. Two of the four cars are open-top double-deckers, which look especially good coming towards you down the street. The best view is from the middle of the shopping street, looking along the track, so the rails lead the eye towards the tram and the shopfronts frame it. Wait for a tram to appear, then take several shots as it approaches. If you have time, try the loop at Plaza Nicky, where an orange tram sits with the track curving round the plaza, or the stretch near Plaza Chipi Chipi. Trams share the street with walkers, so keep to the pavement and stay alert. Running days and the route can change, so check before you go.
text.geographic_location: In the downtown centre of Oranjestad, along Caya Betico Croes, the main shopping street, which is open to pedestrians only. The line starts near the Port of Call Marketplace and ends at Plaza Nicky.
text.directions_text: There are no tram or train stops listed for this spot, so head for downtown Oranjestad and Caya Betico Croes, the main pedestrian shopping street. Once there, walk along the street and follow the track. Plaza Nicky and Plaza Chipi Chipi are both on the line if you want a second angle. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the tram and the street. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit in the full width of the street and the buildings on both sides. Use telephoto (2x to 5x, depending on your phone) when the tram is further away, which squeezes the street together and fills the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Caya Betico Croes (pedestrian mall stretch, facing along the track). A tram rolling down the pedestrianized main shopping street, with the colonial-style downtown buildings lining both sides. Stay on the pavement, not on the rails.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the track on a line so it leads into the picture, with the tram a little off-centre. Keep the buildings upright on both sides. Take a burst or hold the shutter as the tram approaches. A Live Photo can catch the movement. For another view, try Plaza Nicky, where the track curves round the plaza.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tram to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky is bright, so the tram's colours stay rich. Make sure the lens is clean, as street shots in warm, humid air can look hazy.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early or late in the day, when the light is softer and the street is likely to be quieter. Operating days and hours may change, so check with Arubus before you go.

text.access_note: The street is an open public pedestrian space, but the tram's running days, hours and route can change, so check the official Arubus site before you go.

name: Numismatic Museum of Aruba
label: Numismatic Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q3083059: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Coin museum with a large collection from around the world.

text.description: The Numismatic Museum of Aruba (Museo Numismatico Aruba in Papiamento) is a small piece of Oranjestad's cultural history. It was founded by J. Mario Odor and opened on 13 November 1981. Its collections covered coins, paper money and stamps from Aruba and other countries. The museum is now closed, so this is a stop for a photo of the outside and a record of the place, not a visit. Treat it as a quick pause on a walk around town. It suits a simple, honest photo: the building, any signage that remains, and the street around it, which together show how the spot looks today. Because it is no longer a working museum, don't plan on going in, and be tactful if the building is in private use. Start with a wide, steady shot that shows the whole frontage and its surroundings. Then take one or two closer frames of details such as lettering, doors or windows. Keep your phone upright for the building and turn it sideways if you want to include more of the street. Turn on the gridlines so the walls and rooflines sit straight, and keep an eye on passing traffic and people so they don't spoil the frame. If the sun is strong, tap the building to focus and lower the exposure slider a little so the sky doesn't wash out.
text.geographic_location: In the city of Oranjestad, on the island of Aruba.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. Head for the former museum in central Oranjestad using the map, aiming for the phone icon on the map. Once you reach the former museum you are at the spot, so there is no further walk. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the building. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) only if the street is narrow and you cannot fit the frontage in. Use 2x or the telephoto lens for details such as lettering or doorways.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. The map marks the former museum at this same spot, so there is no direction to face. Look around for the building. Step back if there is room to fit more of the scene.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the building's edges with them so the walls look straight. Take one wide frame showing the whole building and its street, then a closer frame of a detail. Keep parked vehicles and passers-by out of the edges where you can.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky is bright so the walls keep their colour. Hold the phone with both hands and take two or three frames to be sure one is sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight, ideally morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and shadows are gentler than at midday.

text.access_note: The museum is now closed, so there is no visit inside; enjoy the outside from the public street and check local information before you go.
